They know it as an American elm; its leaves make us doubt that, so we are asking readers to tell us what it is.

trees.story:
A reader walking the trails of Wilderness Park, the long strip of woodland on Lincoln's southern edge, stopped under this tree and sent us a photograph taken straight up its trunk.

The trunk is the thing. It is thick and deeply furrowed, the grey bark broken into long ridges that cross and rejoin like plaited rope, and it rises a long way before it forks. Above that the limbs open into a high, light crown, the sky showing through everywhere, and against the blue you can see that each leaf is made of many small rounded leaflets.

The reader knows it as an American elm. The leaves in their picture make us doubt that. An elm has single leaves, not rows of leaflets, and those leaflets and that ridged bark look more like a locust or a coffeetree. We would rather ask than guess, so if you walk past it, look at a fallen leaf and tell us here what you think it is, and we will put the right name on the page.

We have no age or girth for it yet either. Stand at its foot and look up, as the reader did.
